whatTheOverrideCosts.statement: The recommendation existed for a reason and the reason does not evaporate because it was overruled. v22's position was that no managed durable user-derived write should happen without an explicit policy. namedExposures: A user who runs the tool once, having configured nothing, has analysis evidence written durably into their project without having been asked first.
Combined with bounds defaulting to unbounded, the default configuration is MAXIMAL retention: keep everything, forever, until someone configures otherwise.
Combined with the append-only ledger, which no bound may touch, a project that is never configured grows monotonically and without limit.
whatMitigatesThem: The ask still happens at the first local-interactive durable-authoritative run, so the un-asked window is bounded by the first interactive use rather than lasting forever.
The default is never persisted, so a user who is later asked answers a genuinely open question rather than confirming something already written on their behalf.
Purge remains available and remains degradation rather than deletion, so retention is reversible in the capability sense even though the tombstone is not.
whatTheOverrideCosts.whatDoesNotMitigateThem: Nothing here reduces what is written before the first ask. The exposure is real, it was stated to the authority in those terms, and the authority accepted it. This artifact records it rather than softening it.

overriddenArchitecturalRecommendation.whatArchitectureMayNotDoAboutIt: It may not re-litigate the decision by designing a mechanism that quietly restores the recommendation -- for instance by defaulting bounds aggressively so that durable-by-default becomes durable-briefly. Bounds default to unbounded precisely so that this artifact does not smuggle back the position the authority rejected.

hasNoDefaultField.whyThatJustificationIsDead: It rested on the choice being unmade. The authority has now made it. The reason the field is still absent is completely different and must not be allowed to inherit the old sentence.
hasNoDefaultField.replacementJustification: The record still has no default field, because a default belongs in a total resolution function where it is stated once and derived, not replicated into every project's record where it could not be told apart from a choice.
hasNoDefaultField.whatIsExplicitlyWithdrawn: the stronger reading that no default exists anywhere in the system. A default now exists. It lives in effective_posture and is named DEFAULTED.

absenceIsADistinctState.withdrawnAsAPostureClaim: Absence no longer means there is no posture. It resolves to DURABLE_RETAINED, the same posture a consenting user would produce.
absenceIsADistinctState.survivesAsAProvenanceClaim: ABSENT and a recorded DURABLE_RETAINED remain genuinely different states. They agree on posture and differ on provenance: DEFAULTED against CONSENTED. The distinction moved from the posture axis to the provenance axis; it did not disappear.
absenceIsADistinctState.whyItMustSurviveSomewhere: Consent provenance is the whole subject of Part A. If ABSENT and CONSENTED DURABLE_RETAINED became the same state, the system would lose the ability to say whether anyone was ever asked, and the first-run ask would become unobservable in its own outputs.

postureEnum.whyNoThirdMember: ABSENT was never a posture enum member and does not become one. It is the absence of a record, and it is now an INPUT to the resolution rather than an output of it. Adding it to the enum would make every consumer branch on a state the resolution exists to remove.

lawFourteenPosition.lawVerbatim: A durability failure cannot report authoritative success; a provider fault cannot become a finding; a policy failure cannot become a host error.
lawFourteenPosition.whatTheDefaultRemoves: the NEED to refuse a durable-authoritative request when no policy exists

Refusing is the only remaining honest option, so the refusal is not a leftover -- it is the case the refusal was always for.
theRefusalPathSurvivesAndMoves.netEffect: The refusal moves from the un-consulted case to the consulted-and-declined case. It becomes rarer and better justified. It does not disappear, and an implementation that deleted it would violate law 14 in the direction the default was never meant to license.

It does not say that an interrupt is a dismissal, and the packet's decision text contains no word about signals at all. Treating SIGINT as a dismissal means Ctrl-C causes a durable write the user was in the middle of not answering, which is surprising enough that it should be decided rather than inherited from a general rule about dismissals.

The ask is performed at most once per request; after it concludes the request proceeds under the resolved effective posture without a second ask. noAskCasesReDerived.name: CI and every other non-interactive invocation
noAskCasesReDerived.predecessorDecisionVerbatim: CI never prompts, never writes a policy and never infers one. It is read-only with respect to the policy. With no policy present, an ephemeral or advisory request proceeds ephemeral and a durable-authoritative request is refused at request-validation.
whatSurvives: CI never infers one -- and this is now sharper, not weaker: resolving ABSENT to DURABLE_RETAINED is not inference, because the resolution is total, stated once, and identical everywhere. Inference would be CI guessing from context.
CI remains read-only with respect to the policy: the ABSENT state on disk is unchanged by any CI run.
An ephemeral or advisory request still proceeds ephemeral.
The A1-RI-04 consistency argument survives intact, including that mere file presence must not become a CI denial-of-service switch.
noAskCasesReDerived.whatChanges: a durable-authoritative request with no policy is no longer refused; it proceeds and writes durably with provenance DEFAULTED
noAskCasesReDerived.whyTheRefusalWasThereBefore: v24's reason was that proceeding would mean choosing a retention default. That was correct while no default existed. A default now exists and was chosen by the authority, so proceeding no longer chooses anything.
noAskCasesReDerived.whatIsNowExposedThatWasNotBefore: CI runs on machines nobody is sitting at, and CI is the profile that can never be asked. So CI is precisely where durable evidence is now written with provenance DEFAULTED and no prospect of the provenance ever becoming CONSENTED by that path. This is the sharpest edge of the posture decision and it is named rather than left implicit.
noAskCasesReDerived.whenRefusalIsStillReachableInCi: when a policy IS present and records EPHEMERAL_ONLY, and the request is durable-authoritative. That cell is unchanged.

noAskCasesReDerived.name: the run that triggers the prompt
noAskCasesReDerived.predecessorChoiceVerbatim: REFUSE-TO-START-UNTIL-ANSWERED, with the ask relocated to request-validation
whatSurvives: The relocation of the ask to request-validation survives completely.

Its justification never rested on the default. It rested on the admission boundary: asking at request-validation means there is no ExecutionId, no AttemptRecord, no SnapshotId, no PlanId, no ExecutionPlan and no Run at ask time, so there is nothing to buffer and nothing to discard.

Both rejected alternatives stay rejected for their original reasons: buffering leaves user-derived evidence in host memory reaching swap and the page cache, which DeletionProtocol cannot erase; discard-and-re-run doubles the work and leaves a partial execution unrecorded.
The ask remains a host effect at request-validation, so freeze law 5 is untouched and the core still never sees the policy or the prompt.
noAskCasesReDerived.whatChanges: REFUSE-TO-START-UNTIL-ANSWERED becomes ASK-BUT-DO-NOT-BLOCK. The question is still asked at the same point; not answering it no longer stops the run.
noAskCasesReDerived.whyTheRelocationStillMattersEvenWithoutT: This is the part most at risk of being discarded as collateral. The relocation was never a mechanism for refusing; it was a mechanism for ensuring the question is asked at a point where the answer can still govern everything that follows. With a default in place the answer governs whether provenance becomes CONSENTED and whether a policy is persisted at all, both of which still need to be settled before an ExecutionId exists. Asking later would mean a run that had already written durably under DEFAULTED asking a question whose answer could no longer change what it did.

whatSurvives: Closing the dialog is still not an answer.

thePolarityReversalThatMattersMost.predecessorReasonVerbatim: A dismissal that silenced the next ask would become EPHEMERAL_ONLY by exhaustion, which is consent obtained by outlasting the user. The ask fires only when a durable-authoritative request needs it, so this is bounded by the user's own requests rather than by a nag timer.
thePolarityReversalThatMattersMost.successorReason: A dismissal that silenced the next ask would become DURABLE_RETAINED by exhaustion: the user is never asked again, and their project is retained durably and unboundedly forever without anyone ever having consented.
thePolarityReversalThatMattersMost.whyThisStrengthensTheRuleRatherThanWeake: Under the old default, exhaustion drifted toward retaining less than the user might have wanted -- an annoyance. Under the new default, exhaustion drifts toward retaining data the user was never asked about -- a consent failure. The same rule, dismissalSuppressesTheNextAsk false, now guards a materially more serious failure, so an implementer tempted to relax it for user-experience reasons should read this paragraph first.

The predecessor of this artifact wrote 'attrition' in both halves and attributed it to v24, which does not contain the token. The parallel construction was therefore manufactured by putting the successor's chosen word into the predecessor's mouth. The substantive polarity reversal was and is real; the attribution was not.

theDefaultIsUnbounded.statedBy: the CD-RT-5 decision at product-dispositions.v1.json#/decisions/CD-RT-5, verbatim: 'A project with no configured retention policy retains durably and unboundedly. A durable-authoritative request with no policy PROCEEDS AND WRITES rather than refusing.'
theDefaultIsUnbounded.whyTheDefaultIsNotWrittenIntoTheRecord: Same reasoning as the posture default: a default written into every project's record cannot be told apart from a choice, and changing it would mean migrating records rather than editing one function. The bounds resolution mirrors the posture resolution exactly.
theDefaultIsUnbounded.whyUnboundedRatherThanTheShippingProduct: The authority said unbounded unless configured. Adopting 200 / 60 days / 150 MB as silent defaults would mean a user who configured nothing nevertheless has evidence purged on a schedule they never chose. It would also quietly restore the position the authority overrode, by making durable-by-default mean durable-for-sixty-days.

effectiveBoundsResolution.signature: effective_bounds(boundsOrAbsent: ProjectRetentionBoundsV1 | ABSENT) -> (maxAgeSeconds, maxTotalBytes, keepCount, provenance: BoundsProvenance)
effectiveBoundsResolution.whyKeepTheDistinctionWhenBothPurgeNothin: The observable purge behaviour is identical today, which is exactly why the distinction must be structural rather than behavioural. If ABSENT were collapsed into all-zero, then the day anyone introduces a non-zero default upstream, every project that never configured retention silently acquires it. Keeping the states distinct means a bound can only ever arrive by someone writing a value into a record someone created. It is also the same consent-provenance shape Part A needs, applied to configuration.

residence.store: host-owned project storage under projects/<ProjectId>/, alongside the project retention policy and the availability ledger
residence.why: This is where the shipping product's shape is NOT adopted. The product keeps these knobs in a configuration file. In this corpus a resolved configuration layer is a place CI cannot see: the freeze records that CI and non-interactive mode never load or resolve layer 4. Bounds in a resolved layer would mean the same project retains different amounts of evidence depending on how it was invoked, invisibly. Host-owned project storage is neither a resolution layer nor inside the analysis snapshot root, so the PlanId exclusion is structural and the value is identical under every invocation profile.

boundsRecord.whyPostureAndConsentAreForbiddenHere: Two provenances must not be mixed in one record. posture and consentRecordRef are CONSENT-derived: they exist because a human was asked a question whose exact text digests into the consent record. maxAgeSeconds, maxTotalBytes and keepCount are CONFIGURATION-derived: nobody is asked. Letting a configuration record carry a posture would let configuration answer the consent question.

identity.preimage: UTF8(domainUtf8) || 0x00 || u16be(recipeVersion=1) || u16be(fieldCount=6) || frame(0x01, projectId) || frame(0x02, retentionPolicyId) || 0x03 || u32be(8) || u64be(maxAgeSeconds) || 0x04 || u32be(8) || u64be(maxTotalBytes) || 0x05 || u32be(8) || u64be(keepCount) || 0x06 || u32be(8) || u64be(boundsRevision)
identity.digest: SHA-256 over the complete preimage; textual form is rbnd1:sha256:<64 lowercase hex>
excluded: the current footprint of the project
any field of any other project's bounds record
identity.separateIdentityRule: Freeze law 6: separate identities keep separate descriptors and separate recipes. This is why the bounds are NOT added as a seventh field of ProjectRetentionPolicyV1. Adding a field there would change that record's field set while RETENTION-POLICY-ID-V1 declares recipeVersion 1 over fieldCount 3, so either the recipe stops describing the record, or the policy identity is re-minted every time an operator adjusts a storage knob.
identity.whyReMintingThePolicyIdentityWouldBeWron: retentionPolicyId is the identity of a CONSENT-bearing record: it is what consentRecordRef and policyRevision hang from. If changing maxTotalBytes re-minted it, an operator lowering a disk cap would produce a new policy identity, and either the consent record would have to be re-obtained for a storage tweak, or the same consent would be re-pointed at a new identity.
identity.preimageFramingRule: frame(tag, s) = tag || u32be(byteLength(NFC UTF-8 s)) || NFC UTF-8 s, identical to RETENTION-POLICY-ID-V1's; the four integer fields use the fixed-width form tag || u32be(8) || u64be(value)

encoderControl.why: a recipe with no worked value cannot be recomputed, and a worked value from an unvalidated encoder cannot be trusted. So the encoder was first required to reproduce a published golden it did not author.
encoderControl.control: RETENTION-POLICY-ID-V1, over v24's own two policyVectors rows

identity.whyThatIsStatedHere: the B1 repair introduces an internal Cap domain with a value, UNBOUNDED, that has no wire encoding. An identity computed over Cap would be unconstructible for any disabled dimension. Controlled by PC-V-20.

referenceDirection.statement: ProjectRetentionBoundsV1 carries retentionPolicyId. ProjectRetentionPolicyV1 carries no reference to the bounds.
referenceDirection.whyNotTheOtherDirection: A pointer from the policy to the bounds would put a mutable configuration digest inside the consent-bearing record, re-minting the policy identity on every knob change. Pointing the other way keeps the mutable thing downstream of the stable thing.
whatThisEnforces: Bounds cannot exist without a policy: a bounds record whose retentionPolicyId names no persisted policy for this projectId is refused at admission.

Bounds cannot outlive the consent they were configured under: when the policy is revised its retentionPolicyId changes, and a bounds record naming the superseded identity is refused until re-stated against the current policy.
Configuration can never answer the consent question, because configuration is the side that must NAME the answer, not the side that supplies it.

interactionWithTheDefaultedPosture.case: a project with no policy at all, whose posture therefore resolves DURABLE_RETAINED with provenance DEFAULTED
interactionWithTheDefaultedPosture.why: There is no persisted policy for a bounds record to name, so no bounds record can be admitted. A defaulted posture is not a persisted policy and does not become one.
interactionWithTheDefaultedPosture.consequence: The default configuration -- durable, unbounded, unasked -- is also the UNBOUNDABLE configuration until someone answers the retention question. A user cannot cap their disk usage without first being asked, or asking, about retention.
interactionWithTheDefaultedPosture.isThatAcceptable: IT IS A CONSEQUENCE, NOT A CHOICE MADE HERE
interactionWithTheDefaultedPosture.whyItIsFlagged: It is the least obvious interaction between the two recorded intents, and it points the wrong way: the configuration most in need of a bound is the one that cannot have one. An alternative -- letting bounds name a projectId rather than a policy identity -- would fix it and would also let configuration exist with no consent record behind it. This artifact does not choose between those; it names the tension.

referenceDirection.statedCost: Re-consenting forces bounds to be re-stated. That is deliberate: a bounds record silently surviving a change of posture would be a configuration outliving the consent that justified it.

protectedSet.derivation: A record is protected exactly when purging it would violate an invariant that already holds. This artifact therefore introduces NO protected list: the protected set is already fully determined by the independently verified Part B.

membersAndTheInvariantThatProtectsThem.member: every entry of UnitAvailabilityLedgerV1, which is to say every tombstone
every one of the 16 members of purgeMutationBoundary.doesNotMutate, including the sealed Run, the closure commitment, the evidence digest, PlanId and SnapshotId
membersAndTheInvariantThatProtectsThem.protectedBy: RT23-B-INV-04, which states that purge mutates exactly two things and no member of doesNotMutate
they are not raw objects in the project CAS; purge acts only on raw object bytes under projects/<ProjectId>/objects/

protectedSet.whyDerivingItMattered: An enumerated protected list would be a second place the truth is written, and the two would drift. Deriving it from doesNotMutate means the protected set changes only when the mutation boundary changes, and the mutation boundary is what a reviewer already checks.

evictableSet.definition: the raw objects under projects/<ProjectId>/objects/ whose current folded availability state is AVAILABLE, in the ledger of exactly this ProjectId
evictableSet.whyFoldedStateAndNotDiskContents: The ledger fold is the authority on what state a raw key is in. A record already PURGED has no bytes to reclaim and re-purging is idempotent, so including it would inflate every demand without freeing anything. A record in MISSING-DEPENDENCY is already absent from CAS. A record in OUTAGE is present but unreadable now.
evictableSet.whyOutageIsNeverEvictable: OUTAGE is reversible and PURGED is terminal. A sweep that evicted during an outage would turn a transient store problem into permanent evidence loss, and the ledger would honestly record it as an authorized retention action, which it was not. This is law 14 applied directly: a provider fault must not become something else.

sweep.theCentralStructuralProperty: A bound is a purge TRIGGER, not an admission GATE. Bounds select what to purge; they have no authority over whether a write is admitted. Everything else in this section follows from that one sentence, including what happens when a bound cannot be satisfied.
sweep.mutationBoundaryUnchanged: purgeMutationBoundary.mutatesExactly still has exactly two members. The sweep is a new CALLER of that boundary, not a new boundary.

neverRunsWhenBoundsAreDefaulted.statement: with provenance DEFAULTED the three configured values are 0, so all three caps lift to UNBOUNDED, every demand evaluates to 0 by the derivation on its own row, evictionCount is max(0, 0, 0) = 0, and the sweep emits nothing
neverRunsWhenBoundsAreDefaulted.isThisComputedOrAsserted: COMPUTED, one step at a time, from the published expressions.
neverRunsWhenBoundsAreDefaulted.whatThePredecessorSaidHere: the same sentence, at $.partC_retentionBounds.sweep.neverRunsWhenBoundsAreDefaulted, asserted rather than derived -- and false of the expressions v25 published, which returned len(evictable) for all three at 0 / 0 / 0.
neverRunsWhenBoundsAreDefaulted.whyThisIsTheMostLoadBearingSentenceInPar: Under the CD-RT-5 decision every project that nobody has configured is durable, unbounded and at 0 / 0 / 0. A defect here is a defect on the default path of every project, and the direction of the predecessor's defect was toward deleting all of their evidence.

evictionOrder.order: ascending atSequence of the raw key's most recent AVAILABLE-entering ledger entry, tiebroken by recordCasRef lexicographic ascending
evictionOrder.adoptedFrom: the shipping product's oldest-first eviction, ordered (timestamp, id) ASC
evictionOrder.departedIn: the ordering key is the project ledger's atSequence, not a wall-clock timestamp
evictionOrder.whyLedgerSequenceRatherThanAClock: atSequence is already specified as strictly increasing by exactly one, with a break refused, so the ledger already carries a total order that is durable, host-owned, monotone and clock-free. A wall clock is none of those: it moves under NTP correction, is not monotone across a restart, and makes eviction order depend on a value no reviewer can reproduce. The tiebreak on recordCasRef makes the order total rather than a preorder, so two hosts folding the same ledger evict the same prefix in the same order.
evictionOrder.whySameOrderForEveryDimension: Derived from the composition requirement, not chosen for efficiency. With ONE order the set each bound wants removed is a PREFIX, and prefixes are totally ordered by inclusion, so the union of several demands is exactly the longest of them. With per-dimension orders the evicted set would be a union of incomparable sets, and disabling one bound could change WHICH records another bound removes rather than merely how many. Independence of bounds is a consequence of the single order.
evictionOrder.statedCostOfTheSingleOrder: Oldest-first is not size-optimal. Freeing N bytes may evict many small old records where one large recent record would have sufficed. Accepted deliberately: evicting largest-first would mean a user's most recent analysis disappears because it was big, which is harder to explain and destroys the prefix property. The shipping product also uses oldest-first for its size pruning, so this is agreement rather than departure.

demands.definition: each bound independently computes a DEMAND: the length of the prefix of the eviction order it requires to be removed

theDisableConvention.problem: 0 is the configured value that DISABLES a dimension, and 0 is also an ordinary point in each dimension's numeric domain. A demand expression written over the RAW configured value therefore has to mean two different things at the same number, and each of the three natural expressions means the wrong one there. At keepCount 0, 'leave keepCount records' is 'leave none'. At maxTotalBytes 0, 'fit within maxTotalBytes' is 'fit within nothing'. At maxAgeSeconds 0, 'older than now minus maxAgeSeconds' is 'older than now', which every already-admitted record is. All three demand the entire evictable set at the value that is supposed to switch them off.
theDisableConvention.whyThatIsTheDangerousDirection: 0 / 0 / 0 is not an edge case. Under the CD-RT-5 decision the default posture is DURABLE_RETAINED and bounds are unconfigured, so 0 / 0 / 0 is the configuration of every project nobody has configured -- the COMMON case, and the one the decision makes common. A wrong value there evicts everything in every unconfigured project, and $.shippingProductEvidence.departed[1].why names that direction as the worst possible one for a silent failure.

thePredecessorsRepairAndWhyItWasRejected.whatV25Did: carried the disable behaviour in a sibling scalar named disabledWhen, sitting outside each expression: 'disabledWhen keepCount == 0', 'disabledWhen maxTotalBytes == 0', 'disabledWhen maxAgeSeconds == 0'.
thePredecessorsRepairAndWhyItWasRejected.verdict: IR-RT25-B1, BLOCKING, and the review was right.
thePredecessorsRepairAndWhyItWasRejected.whyItWasRight: It is the same structural shape as the shipping-product defect this lineage exists to refuse. The product's guard tests ANOTHER dimension's value; v25's guard tests its OWN. Those differ in blast radius, not in kind: in both, the expression published as the rule is wrong at a value the configuration can hold, and a SECOND statement somewhere else is what makes the system behave. v25's own boundIndependence.proof asserted 'Disabling a bound sets its demand to 0', which is false of the expressions v25 published, and 4 of its own 5 arithmetic vectors contradicted them.

measuredReproduction.meaning: the entire evictable set is purged in every unconfigured project

thePredecessorsRepairAndWhyItWasRejected.soTheRepairIsNotToMoveTheGuard: It is to remove the need for one. A guard is a second statement that has to agree with the first, and the whole class of defect is the two disagreeing.

theDisableConvention.repair: ONE total lift, applied identically to all three configured values, before any demand is computed.
theDisableConvention.name: unbounded_if_zero
theDisableConvention.rule: unbounded_if_zero(v) := UNBOUNDED if v == 0 else v
theDisableConvention.capOrder: Cap is totally ordered by <=, with UNBOUNDED strictly greater than every u64. Exactly two arithmetic extensions follow from that order, and they are the only ones needed: (n - UNBOUNDED) is strictly less than 0 for every u64 n, and (now - UNBOUNDED) is strictly less than every representable admission time.
theDisableConvention.whyALiftAndNotAGuard: A guard is a second statement that must agree with the first. A lift is a change of DOMAIN, after which each demand is a single unconditional expression that is correct at every point of that domain including the disable point. There is no second statement to disagree with, no branch to skip, and no question of where to put it. The class is not fixed, it is made unrepresentable -- which is the same move $.partC_retentionBounds.sweep.boundIndependence.theDefectThisRefusesToInherit makes against the product's parasitism, applied one level down to the product's other failure mode.
theDisableConvention.soDisableBecomesATheorem: Under the lift, 'disabling a bound sets its demand to 0' stops being an assertion beside the expressions and becomes a value COMPUTED from them, one derivation per dimension, published below and reproducible by hand.

unboundedIsNotAWireValue.statement: UNBOUNDED is a value of an internal resolution function and is never a value of a record field.
unboundedIsNotAWireValue.whereTheWireStops: ProjectRetentionBoundsV1.maxAgeSeconds, .maxTotalBytes and .keepCount are unsigned integers with minimum 0, admitted at exact JSON type before any content comparison per freeze section 6 law 18. The lift runs strictly after admission, inside effective bounds resolution.
unboundedIsNotAWireValue.whyThatMattersConcretely: RETENTION-BOUNDS-ID-V1 frames each of the four integer fields as u64be. UNBOUNDED has no u64be encoding. If the identity were computed over lifted caps, every project that disabled any dimension would have an unconstructible preimage. It is computed over the configured u64 values, so a disabled dimension frames u64be(0) and the preimage is always exactly 248 bytes for a given projectId and retentionPolicyId. Controlled by PC-V-20.

demands.capResolution: cap_age := unbounded_if_zero(maxAgeSeconds); cap_size := unbounded_if_zero(maxTotalBytes); cap_count := unbounded_if_zero(keepCount)

rows.derivationAtUNBOUNDED: len(evictable) - UNBOUNDED is strictly less than 0 by the Cap order, and max(0, x) = 0 for every x < 0. The 0 is the value of the published expression at the published input; nothing outside the expression is consulted.
rows.whySatisfiable: len(evictable) is a fold of the ledger and needs no input that does not exist

rows.demand: demand_size := the smallest k in [0, len(evictable)] such that total_bytes(evictable[k:]) <= cap_size
mentionsExactly: the eviction order, through total_bytes of its suffixes
rows.derivationAtUNBOUNDED: total_bytes(evictable[0:]) is a u64 and UNBOUNDED is strictly greater than every u64, so k = 0 already satisfies the condition and is the smallest index in the range. The demand is 0 without any case being taken.

aFallbackClauseWasRemovedAndItWasDead.predecessorClauseVerbatim: or len(evictable) if no such k exists
aFallbackClauseWasRemovedAndItWasDead.derivation: at k = len(evictable) the suffix is empty and total_bytes of an empty suffix is 0, which is <= every member of Cap because Cap's u64 part has minimum 0 and UNBOUNDED is above all of it. A satisfying k therefore always exists and the fallback can never be taken.
aFallbackClauseWasRemovedAndItWasDead.whyRemovingItIsWorthRecording: an unreachable branch in a published expression is a branch no vector can exercise and no reviewer can falsify, and it makes the expression look partial when it is total. Removing it is not tidying: it is what lets 'demand_size is total on Cap' be checked rather than believed.

rows.whySatisfiable: the byte length of a raw object is the length of the bytes at projects/<ProjectId>/objects/<recordKind>/sha256/<digestHex>, which the host measures directly; no schema field is required and none is added

rows.demand: demand_time := the number of leading members of the eviction order whose admission time is strictly older than cutoff, where cutoff := now - cap_age
mentionsExactly: the eviction order, through the admission time of its members
rows.derivationAtUNBOUNDED: cutoff = now - UNBOUNDED is strictly less than every representable admission time by the Cap order, so no member is strictly older than it and the leading run has length 0.
rows.whyThisDimensionMattersMostForThisRepair: DEP-RT25-01 forces maxAgeSeconds to 0 and refuses any other value at admission. So 0 is not merely the default of the time dimension, it is its ONLY legal value today. Under the predecessor's published expression that single legal value was the one demanding the whole set. Controlled by PC-V-18.
rows.whyNotSatisfiable: no reviewed surface in this corpus records a per-raw-object admission time; see DEP-RT25-01

demands.whyTheCompositionSurvivedTheRepair: IR-RT25-B1 did not touch it. Its own words: 'the composition is right, the expressions composed are not.' The independent review re-executed the attribution rule and the max-not-sum argument separately and reported both correct at IR-RT25-N08. This repair changes what is composed and changes nothing about how.
demands.evictedSet: the first evictionCount members of the eviction order
demands.whyMaxAndNotSum: Each demand is a prefix LENGTH, not a set. Removing the longest demanded prefix satisfies every shorter demand simultaneously, because a shorter prefix is contained in a longer one. Summing would evict records no bound asked for.

everyDemandIsZeroAtItsOwnDisableValue.theorem: for X in {count, size, time}: demand_X evaluated with cap_X = UNBOUNDED is 0, and cap_X = UNBOUNDED holds exactly when the configured value is 0
everyDemandIsZeroAtItsOwnDisableValue.isThisAssertedOrComputed: COMPUTED. Three derivations, one per dimension, each published on its own row above, each reproducible by hand from the expression and the Cap order.
everyDemandIsZeroAtItsOwnDisableValue.corollaryTheDefaultConfiguration: at 0 / 0 / 0 all three caps are UNBOUNDED, all three demands are 0, and evictionCount is max(0, 0, 0) = 0. The sweep emits nothing. That sentence is now the value of the published expressions at the published default, not a claim placed beside them.

reMeasuredAgainstTheArithmeticVectors.method: this artifact's author implemented the expressions above and re-executed every arithmetic row of $.partC_retentionBounds.vectors against them, under the equal-object-size reading PC-V-04's own note confirms

perRow.causeHere: NONE -- eviction count is 0, so no cause is attributed

reMeasuredAgainstTheArithmeticVectors.whatThisDoesAndDoesNotShow: It shows the published expressions now agree with the published expectations, which is exactly what IR-RT25-B1 found they did not. It does NOT show the expressions are right about storage: the vectors are declared, not executed against a store, and RT25-RES-01 records that no instrument runs any of them. This is arithmetic agreement between two statements by the same author, and IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md section 7.8 is explicit about what that is worth.

boundIndependence.property: each demand is a pure function of exactly two things: the shared eviction order, and that one bound's own lifted cap
boundIndependence.whyThatSentenceIsHere: IR-RT25-B1's fourth ground was that the predecessor's proof was not a proof of what its expressions did: 'Disabling a bound sets its demand to 0 is asserted, not derived from the published expressions, and is false of them. The monotonicity argument that follows is correct about max and irrelevant to the defect.' The monotonicity argument is retained below because it was never the problem; step 2 is the one that had to become true.

proof.step1_symbolInventory: Each published demand expression mentions exactly two kinds of symbol: the shared eviction order, and its own cap. Measured over the three rows: occurrences of another dimension's configured value or lifted cap inside any expression, 0 of 3. There is no term in which one bound's value could appear inside another's.
proof.step2_disableIsComputedNotAsserted: demand_X(cap_X = UNBOUNDED) = 0 for X in {count, size, time}, each derived on its own row from the expression and the Cap order. This is the step the predecessor asserted and could not derive, and it is the step the independent review falsified.
proof.step3_monotonicity: max is monotone in each argument, so evictionCount >= demand_Y for every Y whatever cap_X is. Setting any one cap to UNBOUNDED therefore cannot reduce what any other dimension requires.
proof.step4_independenceIsOfTheSetNotJustTheCo: Because there is ONE total eviction order, every demand is a prefix LENGTH and prefixes are totally ordered by inclusion. So disabling a bound cannot change WHICH records another bound removes, only how many are removed in total. Independence holds of the evicted set, not merely of its size -- which is the property per-dimension orders would lose.
proof.whatWouldFalsifyIt: a demand expression naming a second dimension's cap; a demand whose value at UNBOUNDED is non-zero; or a composition other than max. Each is checkable by reading the three rows above, and PC-V-02, PC-V-03, PC-V-04, PC-V-17 and PC-V-18 exercise them.

theDefectThisRefusesToInherit.shape: the size bound is computed inside the count bound's branch, guarded by a test of the form: if the aggressive keep is <= 0 or the configured keep is <= 1, return early
theDefectThisRefusesToInherit.consequence: with keep set to 0 or 1, maxSizeMb silently deletes nothing; a user who disables count pruning loses size pruning and is not told
theDefectThisRefusesToInherit.whyAListOfPlacesWouldNotHaveFixedIt: The defect is not that one guard sits in the wrong place. It is that the size demand was expressed in terms of the count configuration at all. Enumerating branches to fix leaves the shape that produced them intact. Making each demand a pure function of its own configured value and the shared order makes the class unrepresentable: there is no term in which another bound's value could appear.
theDefectThisRefusesToInherit.structuralPropertyThatReplacesTheList: demand_X depends on X's configured value and the eviction order, and on nothing else

andTheOneThePredecessorReintroduced.found: IR-RT25-B1, the strongest finding of the v25 review
andTheOneThePredecessorReintroduced.shape: the disable behaviour of each dimension sat in a sibling scalar, disabledWhen, beside the expression rather than inside it
andTheOneThePredecessorReintroduced.whyItIsTheSameClassAndNotTheSameSeverity: Same class: in both, the published expression is wrong at a value the configuration can hold, and a second statement elsewhere is what makes the system behave. Different blast radius: the product's guard reads ANOTHER dimension's value, so disabling count silently disables size; v25's guard reads its OWN value, so no dimension could disable another. The review named the class correctly and this artifact does not soften it -- the failure was on the default configuration of every project, which is worse than the product's, whose defect needs someone to have configured keep 0 or 1.
andTheOneThePredecessorReintroduced.whatWasActuallyRepaired: not the placement of the guard. Its existence. There is no guard, in any place, in any of the three expressions.

disableSemantics.zeroMeans: this dimension is UNBOUNDED. The configured 0 is lifted to the Cap value UNBOUNDED before any demand is computed, and each demand expression evaluates to 0 there by its own derivation.
disableSemantics.adoptedFrom: the shipping product, where 0 disables a dimension
disableSemantics.agreesWithTheDefault: the defaulted bounds are 0 / 0 / 0, so the default is expressible in the same vocabulary a user would type
disableSemantics.whatTheProductDoes: a negative or non-finite configured value silently reverts to the built-in default, not to 0
disableSemantics.whyThatIsRefusedHere: Silently substituting a default for an invalid value means a user who typed -1 intending to disable a dimension gets the default bound instead, and their evidence is purged by a rule they explicitly tried to switch off. The failure is silent, the direction is toward MORE deletion, and nothing reports it.
disableSemantics.structuralRepair: There is no code path mapping an invalid value to a valid one, because admission rejects the record before any mapping exists. This is not a check an implementer must remember to write; it is the absence of the substitution.

howAnInvalidConfigurationIsReported.whyNoNewCodeIsRequested: CONFIG.INVALID is already a member of the live closed D9 error-code vocabulary, measured from the pinned bytes. An invalid retention bound is an invalid configuration and needs no new spelling.

anUnsatisfiableBoundIsRefusedNeverIgnore.rule: if maxAgeSeconds is non-zero while no per-raw-object admission time exists, the bounds record is REFUSED at admission with CONFIG.INVALID
anUnsatisfiableBoundIsRefusedNeverIgnore.why: Silently ignoring a bound the system cannot evaluate is the parasitic size bound wearing different clothes: the user configures a limit, the limit does nothing, and nothing says so. Refusing makes the missing input forcing, so the time dimension cannot ship until DEP-RT25-01 is resolved.
anUnsatisfiableBoundIsRefusedNeverIgnore.consequenceStatedPlainly: Until DEP-RT25-01 resolves, maxAgeSeconds can only be 0. The time dimension is specified and unusable. Count, which the shipping product reports as primary, and size are both usable today.

disableSemantics.whereTheDisableBehaviourLives: inside every demand expression, as a value of that expression. Not in a sibling field, not in a guard, and not in a caller.

whenTheBoundCannotBeSatisfied.question: a bound is reached, and the protected set alone exceeds it. Refuse the write, or proceed degraded?
whenTheBoundCannotBeSatisfied.answer: PROCEED. The write is admitted. The sweep evicts everything evictable and stops, because it has run out of things to purge.

whyNotRefuseTheWrite.lawVerbatim: A durability failure cannot report authoritative success; a provider fault cannot become a finding; a policy failure cannot become a host error.
whyNotRefuseTheWrite.argument: A retention bound is a POLICY dimension: it sits in a host-owned, project-scoped record subordinate to a consent-bearing policy. Refusing an analysis write because a retention bound cannot be satisfied converts a policy failure into a host error, which is law 14's third clause named exactly.
After the refusal the bound is still exceeded, byte for byte. Refusal trades a real and recorded degradation for a total loss of function while leaving the storage condition unchanged.

whyNotRefuseTheWrite.reason: the condition is structurally unfixable, so it cannot be a gate
whyNotRefuseTheWrite.argument: The protected set is exactly the ledger plus the 16 members of doesNotMutate, and RT23-B-INV-04 states purge mutates none of them. So when the protected set alone exceeds the bound, no retention policy whatsoever can bring the project under it. A gate whose condition no configuration can satisfy is not a gate, it is an outage with a policy-shaped excuse.

whenTheBoundCannotBeSatisfied.whyNotWarnAndProceedEither: A warning is not an addressable state. It goes to a log, it is not derivable by a second reader, and nothing can be asserted about it. The product's oversize_unresolved is a string in a stream.

whatIsDoneInstead.predicate: over_bound(project) := footprint(project) > maxTotalBytes AND evictable(project) is empty
whatIsDoneInstead.why: Both operands are already readable: the footprint is measurable from the project store and the evictable set is a fold of the ledger. A recorded shortfall event would be a fourth thing that can go stale.
whatIsDoneInstead.consistencyWithSection46: This is the identical move section 4.6 verified for capability: do not record a derived fact, derive it at read time from state that cannot go stale. A second reader computes the same over_bound answer from the same bytes without consulting anything this artifact writes.

overBoundDoesNotLowerCapability.statement: being over bound is not an evidence-semantics condition and must not touch effectiveCapability
overBoundDoesNotLowerCapability.why: Over bound with nothing evictable means the project holds MORE evidence than it asked to keep. Every object is still AVAILABLE, so every unit_satisfied predicate still holds and the derivation still returns the sealed ceiling. Nothing is missing, nothing is refused, no caller is misled. It is a disk-space fact and belongs to operability.

scope.derivation: A global bound is structurally unrepresentable in this corpus, not merely undesirable. Computing a global demand requires aggregating across project ledgers. answeredQuestions.question: What fires when a bound is reached and the protected set alone exceeds it? Refuse the write, or proceed degraded?

Refusing converts a policy failure into a host error against law 14, reclaims no bytes, and gates on a condition that RT23-B-INV-04 makes structurally unsatisfiable. Deriving rather than recording the shortfall is the same move section 4.6 verified for effectiveCapability.

The consequence — no global disk ceiling, and under durable-and-unbounded-by-default an unbounded aggregate across unconfigured projects — is declared as DEP-RT25-03.

answeredQuestions.question: What is the eviction order, and is it the same for every dimension?
answeredQuestions.answer: Ascending atSequence of the raw key's most recent AVAILABLE-entering ledger entry, tiebroken by recordCasRef ascending. One order, shared by every dimension.
answeredQuestions.justification: oldest-first is adopted from the shipping product; the ordering KEY departs from it, using the ledger sequence rather than a wall clock so the order is monotone, durable and reproducible. The sharing is derived: with one order each demand is a prefix length, prefixes are totally ordered by inclusion, and the union of demands is exactly the longest — which is what makes the bounds independent. Per-dimension orders would let disabling one bound change which records another removes.

answeredQuestions.question: Does the tombstone itself ever expire?
answeredQuestions.answer: No. Never. A tombstone is a ledger entry and the ledger is append-only, so expiring one would violate an invariant that already holds and was independently verified against hostile ledgers.
answeredQuestions.justification: this needs no new rule: RT23-B-INV-06 and ledger.entriesAreNeverEditedOrRemoved already forbid it. If a tombstone expired, a purged record would become indistinguishable from a record that never existed, and P2-FLOOR — that no availability state removes the sealed record — would be violated in substance even where it held in letter.

storageConsequenceStatedHonestly.whatMaxTotalBytesActuallyBounds: the object store, NOT the project's total footprint. A project under sustained retention pressure has a monotonically growing ledger that no bound touches.
storageConsequenceStatedHonestly.theRatioIsFavourableButItIsARatioNotABou: an AvailabilityTransitionV1 is a fixed seven-field record dominated by one digest, while the objects it replaces are arbitrary in size. So the store shrinks dramatically under sweeping. It does not shrink to zero and it never stops growing.
storageConsequenceStatedHonestly.noNumberIsInvented: this artifact states no byte size for a tombstone, because that requires an encoding this artifact does not specify. The ratio is claimed qualitatively and no figure is asserted.
storageConsequenceStatedHonestly.growthIsBoundedOnlyBy: the number of purge events, which is bounded by the number of distinct raw keys ever admitted to the project — finite at any instant, unbounded over time
storageConsequenceStatedHonestly.compoundedByThePostureDecision: durable-by-default and unbounded-by-default mean the default project accumulates objects and never sweeps, so the ledger grows only when someone configures a bound. The unbounded growth therefore arrives with the first configured bound rather than on day one — later, and after the user has opted into retention management, which is the better of the two orderings.
storageConsequenceStatedHonestly.whyThisIsTheCorrectTradeAnyway: the decision states, verbatim, 'A tombstone outlives the bytes it describes. Absence is therefore always explainable, and 'purged under policy' is never indistinguishable from 'never existed'.' An explanation that can itself be purged is not an explanation. Unbounded ledger growth is the price of that guarantee and it is the right price, but it must be sized by whoever operates it.
storageConsequenceStatedHonestly.compactionIsNotDesignedHere: a compaction scheme would have to decide what may be forgotten, which is the tombstone-survival question the decision answers no to. So the residual is a consequence of the decision, not a defect in it.

answeredQuestions.question: Are bounds independent? Disabling one must not silently disable another.
answeredQuestions.answer: Yes, by construction. Each demand is a pure function of the shared eviction order and that bound's own configured value, and the demands compose by max.
answeredQuestions.justification: max is monotone in each argument, so setting any one demand to 0 cannot reduce what the others require. The shipping product's defect is not repaired by fixing branches but by removing the shape that let one bound's value appear inside another's expression. Disabling is explicit (0), and an invalid or unsatisfiable value is refused rather than defaulted or skipped, so the two other ways a bound can silently stop working are closed as well.

quotationDiscipline.why: IR-RT25-B4 was blocking because a field named Verbatim asserts a fact about bytes, and two of the predecessor's nineteen were false on those bytes. quotationDiscipline.method: every field in these bytes whose key ends in 'verbatim' was extracted, folded, and searched for in the folded text of THE SOURCE ITS OWN NAME OR POSITION ATTRIBUTES IT TO -- not in a union of every source. Folding follows freeze section 7.7: NFKC normalisation, unicode punctuation normalised to ASCII, markdown structure characters (blockquote markers, emphasis, backticks, table pipes, backslashes) replaced by spaces, whitespace collapsed, case folded. Section 7.7 records that a byte-literal search on a multi-word phrase returns a false ABSENT on line-wrapped text, and that whitespace normalisation ALONE still returns ABSENT on a blockquote.

whyScopedAndNotUnionWide.statement: A union-wide search cannot see an INHERITED misquotation.
whyScopedAndNotUnionWide.howThisWasLearned: not by reasoning. A companion instrument for the predecessor, check-retention-custody-v25.py, was written by another lane and reports it directly: d9OwnRuleVerbatim misquotes D9, and that misquotation was already carried by retention-tiers.v23 and .v24, so a corpus-wide token search FINDS the text and reports nothing. The first build of these bytes used exactly that union-wide search and reported 37 of 37 verified. The scoped search was then written and run, and it also reports 37 of 37 -- but the two results are not the same claim, and only the second one is the claim this field makes.
whyScopedAndNotUnionWide.andItFoundAThirdInstanceTheReviewDidNotR: the same instrument reports a THIRD field of the predecessor as a B4 instance: $.productAuthorityBoundary.packetRuleWhilePendingVerbatim, 'No implementer may choose a retention default and no freeze may claim V10 resolved.', attributed by its own name to product-dispositions.v1.json and absent from that file. Measured here independently: the string does not occur in the packet, and does occur in five other files. The independent review found two instances; the scoped instrument finds three. That field does not exist in these bytes at all -- $.productAuthorityBoundary was rewritten wholesale to record the decision -- so the third instance is repaired by removal rather than by correction, and it is recorded here so the repair is not mistaken for luck.

quotationDiscipline.whyThatLastNumberMatters: a field that fails the scoped test but passes a union-wide one is an inherited misquotation, which is the class that survives longest because every predecessor corroborates it
quotationDiscipline.whatAFailureHereWouldMean: a field asserting verbatimness whose text is not in the source it names. That is exactly IR-RT25-B4, and the check is published as data rather than described so a reviewer can re-run it rather than trust it.
whatThisCheckDoesNotEstablish: It does not check that a quotation is COMPLETE or that its elisions are marked. Where a field quotes a complete field value this artifact says so with a quotedSpan marker; where it does not, a reviewer must check the span by hand. IR-RT25-B4's first instance was a truncation as well as a substitution, and containment is monotone -- a truncated quotation still passes a containment test.

It does not check that the ATTRIBUTION MAP is right. The map is written by this artifact's author, and a field attributed to the wrong source would be verified against the wrong file. The map is published in the results so a reviewer can check the attribution separately from the containment.

It ran once, at authoring, in a process nobody can re-execute. Freeze section 7.2.2's bound applies exactly: a reviewer can verify the property this produced; it cannot verify that it ran. Re-running it is one pass over these bytes and the sources listed above.
